sections.overview: The pine looper is a geometrid moth of European and northern Eurasian conifer forests; caterpillars eat pine needles and can periodically defoliate woodland.
sections.identification: Males are slender and brownish with comb-like antennae; broader females are paler and bear a white forewing patch.
sections.habitat: It is associated chiefly with Scots pine, though larvae also feed on other conifers such as lodgepole pine, spruce and larch.
sections.diet: Caterpillars consume needles; severe feeding removes foliage and can reduce growth or kill weakened trees.
sections.behavior: Populations sometimes undergo multi-year outbreaks, particularly in susceptible pine plantations, where repeated feeding can cause extensive defoliation.
sections.reproduction: Usually one generation develops annually: eggs are laid on needles, larvae feed in summer and autumn, and pupae overwinter among fallen needles or debris.
sections.ecology: Its forestry impacts overlap with Panolis flammea, another pine-needle feeder, although the two differ taxonomically and in life cycle.
sections.conservation: It is not generally considered threatened; during outbreaks it is monitored as a forest pest, with damage depending on moth density, tree condition and site.
